Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

A space-based gravitational microlensing exoplanet survey will provide a statistical census of exoplanets with masses down to 0.1 Earth-masses and orbital separations ranging from 0.5AU to infinity. This includes analogs to all the Solar System's planets except for Mercury, as well as most types of planets predicted by planet formation theories. Such a survey will provide results on the frequency of planets around all types of stars except those with short lifetimes. Close-in planets with separations < 0.5 AU are invisible to a space-based microlensing survey, but these can be found by Kepler. Other methods, including ground-based microlensing, cannot approach the comprehensive statistics on the mass and semi-major axis distribution of extrasolar planets that a space-based microlensing survey will provide. The terrestrial planet sensitivity of a ground-based microlensing survey is limited to the vicinity of the Einstein radius at 2-3 AU, and space-based imaging is needed to identify and determine the mass of the planetary host stars for the vast majority of planets discovered by microlensing. Thus, a space-based microlensing survey is likely to be the only way to gain a comprehensive understanding of the nature of planetary systems, which is needed to understand planet formation and habitability. The proposed Microlensing Planet Finder (MPF) mission is an example of a space-based microlensing survey that can accomplish these objectives with proven technology and a cost that fits comfortably under the NASA Discovery Program cost cap.

Its detections would include counterparts to every planet in our Solar System other than Mercury, along with most planet categories anticipated by theories of planet formation. outputs.L3:
A space-based gravitational microlensing exoplanet survey would provide one of the most comprehensive statistical censuses of planetary systems yet envisioned. By monitoring dense star fields from space with high precision and continuous coverage, such a survey could detect planets with masses as low as about 0.1 Earth masses. It would also be sensitive to planets over a very broad range of orbital separations, from roughly 0.5 astronomical units (AU) outward to planets on extremely wide or even unbound orbits. This means that the survey would probe not only planets similar to those in the inner and outer regions of our own Solar System, but also free-floating planets that may have been ejected from their original systems.

A survey of this kind would be capable of detecting analogs of nearly all the planets in the Solar System, with the main exception of Mercury, whose low mass and very small orbital separation make it difficult to detect through microlensing. It would be sensitive to planets resembling Venus, Earth, Mars, the gas giants, and the ice giants, as well as many classes of planets that do not exist in our Solar System but are predicted by planet formation theories. These include super-Earths, cold terrestrial planets, Neptune-like planets at several AU, gas giants beyond the snow line, and planets at very large separations from their host stars. As a result, the survey would test a wide range of theoretical models describing how planetary systems form and evolve.

One of the major strengths of space-based microlensing is that it can measure planet occurrence rates around nearly all types of stars. Because microlensing does not rely on detecting light from the host star itself, it can find planets orbiting faint, distant, or low-mass stars that are difficult to study with other techniques. This includes planets around M dwarfs, main-sequence stars, and even stellar remnants, depending on the event. In this respect, microlensing provides a powerful complement to transit surveys such as Kepler. Kepler is especially effective at finding close-in planets with orbital separations below about 0.5 AU, while microlensing is most sensitive to planets farther from their stars. Together, the two approaches can build a much more complete picture of planetary demographics across a wide range of masses, separations, and stellar environments.

Ground-based microlensing surveys have already demonstrated the power of the technique, but they cannot match the precision, stability, angular resolution, and uninterrupted monitoring possible from space. Earth’s atmosphere, weather, day-night cycles, and crowding in dense stellar fields limit the sensitivity of ground-based observations, particularly for low-mass planets. Other detection techniques, such as radial velocity measurements, direct imaging, and transit surveys, are also valuable but are restricted to particular ranges of planet mass, orbital distance, host-star brightness, or system geometry. Consequently, none of these methods alone can provide the same broad and statistically complete measurement of planetary mass and orbital separation distributions that a dedicated space-based microlensing survey could achieve.

The Microlensing Planet Finder mission has been proposed as a feasible way to carry out such a survey. Designed specifically for space-based microlensing observations, it would monitor large numbers of stars toward the Galactic bulge with the sensitivity and cadence needed to detect planetary signals across the desired mass and orbital-separation range. The mission concept is presented as capable of achieving these scientific goals while remaining within the cost constraints of NASA’s Discovery Program. If implemented, it would provide a fundamental census of planetary systems, offering crucial data for understanding how common different types of planets are and how planetary systems like—and unlike—our own form throughout the Galaxy.
outputs.L4:
A space-based gravitational microlensing survey would be a powerful way to discover and characterize planets that are difficult or impossible to find with other techniques. One example of such a mission is the proposed Microlensing Planet Finder, a dedicated space telescope designed to monitor dense star fields toward the center of the Milky Way. By observing the temporary brightening of background stars caused by the gravity of foreground stars and their planets, such a survey could statistically detect exoplanets with masses as small as about 0.1 Earth masses. Its sensitivity would extend over a very wide range of orbital separations, from roughly 0.5 AU outward to planets at extremely large distances, including planets that are only weakly bound to their stars or even free-floating.

This capability would strongly complement the discoveries made by missions such as Kepler. Kepler was especially effective at finding planets that pass in front of, or transit, their host stars, making it most sensitive to planets on relatively short-period orbits close to their stars. Microlensing, by contrast, is most sensitive to planets located farther from their host stars, especially near and beyond the region where many planetary systems are expected to form giant planets and icy worlds. Together, transit surveys and microlensing surveys would provide a much more complete census of planetary systems, from hot close-in planets to cold planets in wider orbits.

A space-based microlensing mission would also have several advantages over ground-based surveys. Observing from space would provide sharper images, more stable observing conditions, and continuous access to crowded stellar fields that are difficult to study from the ground. These advantages would make it possible to detect subtle microlensing signals from low-mass planets and to measure planet frequencies with high statistical precision. Because microlensing does not depend strongly on the light emitted by the host star, it can detect planets around a broad range of stellar types, including low-mass stars, faint stars, and distant stars that are challenging for other methods.

The scientific value of such a survey would not be limited to individual discoveries. Its greatest contribution would be a comprehensive statistical measurement of how common planets are across a wide range of masses, separations, and host-star environments. It could determine the frequency of terrestrial planets, super-Earths, ice giants, gas giants, and free-floating planets. It would also help reveal how planetary systems differ between various stellar populations in the Galaxy.

These measurements are essential for understanding how planetary systems form and evolve. The distribution of planets as a function of mass and orbital distance provides direct clues about the processes of planet formation, migration, and dynamical evolution. In particular, the abundance of cold terrestrial and giant planets at moderate to large separations would test competing theories of how planets grow from disks of gas and dust around young stars. The detection, or absence, of large populations of free-floating planets would also inform models of planet scattering and ejection.

Such a mission would also contribute to the broader question of habitability. Although microlensing is not generally designed to study planetary atmospheres or search directly for life, it can determine how common potentially habitable worlds may be in the Galaxy. By measuring the occurrence of low-mass planets at separations relevant to temperate or icy environments, it would provide crucial context for future missions that aim to characterize Earth-like planets in detail.

For these reasons, a space-based gravitational microlensing survey would be an essential component of a complete exoplanet exploration program. By filling the discovery space left open by transit and radial-velocity surveys, it would provide the broad statistical foundation needed to understand the architecture of planetary systems and the conditions under which habitable worlds may arise.

counterfactuals.prompt: Summarize the scientific case for a space-based gravitational microlensing mission for detecting exoplanets, including its sensitivity range and how it compares to Kepler and ground-based microlensing.
counterfactuals.output:
A space-based gravitational microlensing mission would provide a census of exoplanets in parts of parameter space that are difficult or impossible to reach with other methods, especially cold, low-mass planets at and beyond the “snow line,” planets around faint or distant stars, and potentially free-floating planets.

## Scientific case

Gravitational microlensing occurs when a foreground star passes close to the line of sight to a more distant background star. The foreground star’s gravity magnifies the background star’s light. If the lens star has a planet, the planet can produce a short-lived perturbation in the magnification pattern. The signal does not require detecting light from the planet or even from the host star, making microlensing especially powerful for distant, faint, or low-mass planetary systems.

A space-based microlensing survey, such as the Roman Space Telescope microlensing program concept, would monitor dense stellar fields toward the Galactic bulge with high cadence, high angular resolution, and stable photometry. This enables detection of thousands of microlensing events and hundreds to thousands of planets, depending on survey design and planet occurrence rates.

Its key scientific goals would be to:

- Measure the frequency of planets beyond the snow line.
- Detect low-mass planets, potentially down to Mars-mass or below in favorable cases.
- Probe planets at orbital separations of roughly ~0.5 AU to several AU, and in projection out to wide separations.
- Detect or constrain free-floating planets, including possibly Earth-mass or sub-Earth-mass objects if sufficiently common.
- Measure the distribution of planet masses and separations in a regime complementary to transit and radial-velocity surveys.
- Provide demographic information across a large range of host stars, including M dwarfs and stars in the Galactic disk and bulge.

## Sensitivity range

A space microlensing mission is most sensitive to planets near the Einstein radius of the lens system, which typically corresponds to projected separations of order a few AU for Galactic bulge events. This is close to or beyond the snow line for many host stars.

Approximate sensitivity includes:

- Planet masses: from gas giants down to super-Earths, Earth-mass planets, and in some cases Mars-mass planets.
- Orbital separations: roughly ~0.5–10 AU for bound planets, with strongest sensitivity around ~1–5 AU.
- Wide-separation and free-floating planets: detectable through short-timescale microlensing events, with sensitivity depending on cadence and photometric precision.
- Host stars: broad sensitivity to stars from low-mass M dwarfs to solar-type stars, including systems too distant or faint for most other planet-detection techniques.

This makes space microlensing one of the best methods for measuring the occurrence rate of cold terrestrial and ice-giant planets.

## Comparison with Kepler

Kepler was primarily a transit survey. It was most sensitive to planets that pass in front of their host stars as seen from Earth, especially planets on short-period orbits.

Kepler’s strengths:

- Excellent sensitivity to close-in planets.
- Large statistical sample of planets with periods from days to months.
- Strong constraints on Earth-size planets in compact inner systems.
- Precise planet radii when host stars are characterized.

Kepler’s limitations:

- Transit probability decreases with orbital distance.
- Long-period planets require many years of monitoring to confirm.
- Weak sensitivity to planets beyond ~1 AU, especially around Sun-like stars.
- Little direct sensitivity to free-floating planets.

Space microlensing is complementary:

- It is most sensitive to planets at ~1–several AU, where Kepler’s sensitivity declines.
- It measures planet mass ratios and, with additional information, planet masses.
- It can detect planets around very faint or distant stars.
- It can detect free-floating planets.
- It probes the cold-planet population beyond the snow line, which is essential for understanding planet formation.

In short, Kepler mapped the inner planetary systems; space microlensing maps the colder outer regions.

## Comparison with ground-based microlensing

Ground-based microlensing surveys have already demonstrated the technique and have detected many planets, including super-Earths and cold planets beyond the snow line. Networks such as OGLE, MOA, KMTNet, and follow-up collaborations monitor the Galactic bulge and can achieve high cadence over wide fields.

However, ground-based microlensing faces major limitations:

- Atmospheric seeing blends many stars together in crowded bulge fields.
- Weather and day-night cycles reduce continuous coverage.
- Optical extinction toward the Galactic bulge limits access to some fields.
- Photometric precision is limited by atmosphere and crowding.
- Short planetary perturbations, especially from low-mass planets, can be missed.
- Lens-source separation and host characterization are harder from the ground.

A space mission improves on this by providing:

- Stable, uninterrupted high-cadence monitoring.
- Much sharper imaging, reducing stellar blending.
- Near-infrared observations, allowing access to heavily extincted bulge fields.
- Better sensitivity to low-mass planets.
- Better characterization of lens stars through high-resolution imaging and astrometric information.
- Improved sensitivity to short-timescale events from free-floating or very low-mass planets.

Thus, ground-based surveys are powerful for discovering microlensing planets, but a space-based survey would turn microlensing into a precision demographic tool.

## Overall significance

A space-based gravitational microlensing mission would fill a major gap in exoplanet demographics. Kepler and similar transit missions reveal the abundance of close-in planets; radial-velocity surveys probe nearby systems mostly within a few AU; direct imaging is sensitive mainly to young, massive planets at wide separations. Space microlensing uniquely probes cold planets of low mass at several AU and free-floating planets across the Galaxy.

Together with Kepler, radial velocity, direct imaging, and ground-based microlensing, a space microlensing mission would help produce a nearly complete statistical picture of planetary systems from hot close-in worlds to cold outer planets and unbound planetary-mass objects.

counterfactuals.prompt: Explain what kinds of planets a space-based microlensing exoplanet survey can detect, what its limitations are, and why it is important for understanding planet formation and habitability.
counterfactuals.output:
A space-based microlensing exoplanet survey detects planets by watching for brief gravitational “lensing” events: when a foreground star passes nearly in front of a more distant background star, the foreground star’s gravity magnifies the background star’s light. If the foreground star has a planet, the planet can add a short, distinctive perturbation to the light curve.

## What kinds of planets it can detect

A space-based microlensing survey is especially good at finding planets that are hard to detect by other methods:

- **Cold planets far from their stars**  
  Microlensing is most sensitive to planets at roughly the scale of the “snow line” and beyond, where ices can form. This includes analogs of Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune, as well as smaller icy worlds.

- **Low-mass planets, including Earth-mass planets**  
  From space, the survey can monitor many faint, crowded stars with high precision, allowing detection of planets down to Earth mass or even below in favorable cases.

- **Planets around distant stars**  
  Microlensing surveys can probe planets thousands of light-years away, especially toward the dense stellar fields of the Galactic bulge. This gives a view of planet populations across a large part of the Milky Way.

- **Planets around a wide range of host stars**  
  The method can find planets around ordinary main-sequence stars, low-mass M dwarfs, and in some cases stellar remnants such as white dwarfs.

- **Free-floating planets**  
  Microlensing can detect planets that are not bound to any star, or are on very wide orbits, because the planet itself can act as the lens. These events are typically short, lasting hours to a day.

- **Multi-planet systems in some cases**  
  If more than one planet produces detectable perturbations during the same microlensing event, the survey can identify multiple planets around the same host.

## Limitations of microlensing surveys

Despite its strengths, microlensing has important limitations:

- **Events are usually one-time and non-repeatable**  
  The lensing alignment happens by chance and generally does not repeat. Unlike transits or radial-velocity signals, the same planet usually cannot be observed orbit after orbit.

- **Limited orbital information**  
  Microlensing often measures the planet-to-star mass ratio and projected separation at the time of the event, not the full orbit. Determining the planet’s exact mass, semimajor axis, eccentricity, and inclination can require additional observations or modeling.

- **Host stars can be difficult to characterize**  
  Many lens stars are faint and distant, and their light may be blended with unrelated stars in crowded fields. Space-based imaging helps, but host properties can still be uncertain.

- **Most detected planets are relatively distant**  
  Microlensing mainly surveys stars toward the Galactic bulge, so many discoveries are thousands of light-years away. These planets are generally not suitable for atmospheric follow-up or direct imaging.

- **Low sensitivity to close-in planets**  
  Microlensing is not the best method for finding very short-period planets close to their stars, such as hot Jupiters or many planets in the classical habitable zones of Sun-like stars. Transit and radial-velocity surveys are better for those.

- **Detection depends on chance alignments**  
  Microlensing events are rare, so surveys must monitor enormous numbers of stars continuously and precisely.

## Why space-based microlensing is important

A space telescope improves microlensing in several key ways:

- It avoids atmospheric blurring, allowing precise measurements in extremely crowded star fields.
- It can detect fainter source stars and smaller planetary signals.
- It provides stable, continuous observations that improve event characterization.
- It can help measure lens brightness and motion, improving estimates of planet and host-star masses.

## Importance for planet formation

Microlensing probes a region of planetary systems that is central to planet formation theory: the cold outer regions around and beyond the snow line. This is where solid material is more abundant because water and other volatiles freeze into ice, helping planetary cores grow.

By measuring how common different planet masses and separations are, microlensing can test key ideas such as:

- how often gas giants form,
- whether Neptune-like and super-Earth planets are common in cold orbits,
- how planet frequency depends on host-star mass,
- how many planets are ejected from systems,
- how planetary architectures differ between the inner and outer regions.

Together with transit and radial-velocity surveys, microlensing helps build a more complete census of planets from hot close-in worlds to cold outer planets.

## Importance for habitability

Microlensing is not primarily an atmospheric or biosignature technique, but it matters for habitability in broader ways:

- It measures the abundance of Earth-mass and super-Earth planets in cold orbits.
- It helps determine how common planetary systems like our own are.
- It constrains the frequency of giant planets, which can influence the delivery of water and the dynamical stability of inner rocky planets.
- It can reveal free-floating planets, some of which might retain subsurface oceans under thick ice or atmospheres.
- It informs models of how water-rich planets form and migrate.

In short, a space-based microlensing survey is important because it fills in a major missing part of the exoplanet census: cold, low-mass, distant, and even free-floating planets. This is essential for understanding how planetary systems form and how common potentially habitable environments may be in the Galaxy.

counterfactuals.prompt: Describe the advantages of space-based gravitational microlensing over other exoplanet detection methods for measuring the mass and semi-major axis distribution of planets around different types of stars.
counterfactuals.output:
Space-based gravitational microlensing has several important advantages for measuring the **planet mass** and **semi-major axis distribution** across a wide range of host-star types, especially compared with transits, radial velocities, and direct imaging.

### 1. Sensitivity to planets at moderate to wide orbital separations

Microlensing is most sensitive to planets near the lens star’s Einstein radius, which typically corresponds to orbital separations of roughly

\[
\sim 1\text{–}10 \ \mathrm{AU}
\]

for typical Galactic lens stars. This is a key region because it overlaps the expected location of the **snow line**, where planet formation efficiency is high.

This gives microlensing a strong advantage over:

- **Transits**, which are most sensitive to close-in planets with short orbital periods.
- **Radial velocities**, which are also most efficient for close-in or moderately separated planets and require long time baselines for wide-orbit planets.
- **Direct imaging**, which is mainly sensitive to massive planets at large separations, often tens of AU.

Thus, microlensing probes a region of planet parameter space that is difficult for other methods.

---

### 2. Sensitivity to low-mass planets

Microlensing can detect planets with masses down to Earth mass and, from space, potentially even below Earth mass under favorable conditions. The signal depends primarily on the planet-to-star mass ratio rather than the planet’s luminosity.

This means microlensing can detect:

- Cold super-Earths
- Earth-mass planets beyond the snow line
- Neptune-mass and Saturn-mass planets at several AU
- Jupiter analogs
- Potentially free-floating or very wide-separation planets

This is difficult for direct imaging, which favors young, hot, massive planets, and for radial velocity surveys, where low-mass planets at wide separations produce very small and slow stellar reflex motions.

---

### 3. Ability to detect planets around faint and distant stars

Microlensing does not require detecting light from the planet or, in many cases, even much light from the host star. The planet is detected through its gravitational effect on the light of a background source star.

As a result, microlensing is sensitive to planets orbiting:

- Low-mass M dwarfs
- K dwarfs and G dwarfs
- Fainter stars in the Galactic disk and bulge
- Stellar remnants such as white dwarfs, neutron stars, or black holes, in some cases

This is a major advantage over radial velocity and transit surveys, which are usually most effective for relatively bright, nearby stars.

Space-based microlensing surveys can therefore measure planet occurrence around stars at different locations in the Galaxy, including the Galactic bulge and disk.

---

### 4. Better mass measurements than ground-based microlensing alone

A major limitation of traditional ground-based microlensing is that it often measures the planet-to-star mass ratio but not the absolute planet mass. A space-based mission can improve this in several ways.

From space, one can often measure or constrain:

- The angular Einstein radius
- The microlens parallax
- The lens flux after or during the event
- The lens-source relative proper motion

These measurements help determine:

\[
M_{\star}
\]

the host-star mass, and therefore

\[
M_p = q M_{\star}
\]

where \(q\) is the measured planet-to-star mass ratio.

Thus, space-based microlensing can turn relative planet detections into a true **planet mass distribution**.

---

### 5. Improved semi-major axis estimates

Microlensing directly measures the projected planet-star separation in units of the Einstein radius:

\[
s R_E
\]

To convert this to a physical separation and ultimately infer a semi-major axis distribution, one needs information about the lens mass and distance. Space-based observations improve those estimates through parallax, high angular resolution, and lens flux measurements.

This allows better statistical reconstruction of the underlying distribution of planets as a function of semi-major axis, especially at separations beyond those well covered by transits and radial velocities.

---

### 6. High angular resolution and reduced blending

In crowded fields toward the Galactic bulge, ground-based observations suffer from severe blending: light from many stars falls into the same seeing disk. This makes it harder to determine the properties of the source and lens stars.

Space telescopes avoid atmospheric seeing and provide much sharper images. This helps by:

- Separating the lens and source light more cleanly
- Measuring lens flux
- Identifying the host-star type
- Reducing false or ambiguous interpretations
- Improving event photometry

This is crucial for determining how planet occurrence depends on stellar mass and Galactic environment.

---

### 7. Continuous, high-precision monitoring

A space-based microlensing survey can observe dense stellar fields continuously with high photometric precision and without interruptions from weather, daylight, or variable seeing.

This is especially valuable because planetary microlensing signals can be short-lived, lasting from days down to hours. Continuous monitoring improves sensitivity to:

- Low-mass planets
- Short planetary perturbations
- Free-floating planet candidates
- Complex multi-planet lensing events

Ground-based surveys can miss or incompletely sample such short signals.

---

### 8. Sensitivity to free-floating and wide-orbit planets

Microlensing is one of the few methods capable of detecting planets that are not close to a luminous host star.

It can detect:

- Free-floating planets
- Planets on very wide orbits
- Planets whose host stars are too faint to detect directly

This provides information about the low-mass end of planet formation and dynamical evolution, including ejection processes.

Transits and radial velocities generally cannot detect truly free-floating planets, while direct imaging is limited to relatively nearby, young, and massive objects.

---

### 9. Less bias toward luminous or active host stars

Radial velocity surveys can be limited by stellar activity, rotation, and spectral line quality. Transit surveys favor stars where small dips can be measured with high precision and where many transits occur during the survey lifetime.

Microlensing selection is different: it depends mainly on the alignment of a foreground lens star with a background source. Therefore, it provides a complementary and less luminosity-biased census of planets.

This is especially important for comparing planet populations around:

- M dwarfs
- Solar-type stars
- More massive main-sequence stars
- Stellar remnants

---

### 10. A Galactic-scale planet census

Because microlensing events occur over kiloparsec distances, a space-based microlensing survey can study planet occurrence across large parts of the Milky Way. This makes it possible to investigate whether planet populations vary with:

- Host-star mass
- Galactic disk versus bulge environment
- Metallicity
- Stellar age
- Distance from the Galactic center

Other methods are mostly restricted to the solar neighborhood, especially radial velocity and direct imaging surveys.

---

## Summary

Space-based gravitational microlensing is especially powerful because it can detect low-mass planets at separations of a few AU around faint and distant stars. It complements transits and radial velocities, which are strongest for close-in planets, and direct imaging, which favors massive planets at wide separations.

Its main advantages for measuring the planet mass and semi-major axis distribution are:

- Sensitivity to Earth- to Jupiter-mass planets beyond the snow line
- Access to planets around faint, low-mass, and distant stars
- Better absolute mass measurements through parallax and lens-flux constraints
- Improved estimates of physical orbital separations
- Reduced blending and higher precision from space
- Continuous monitoring of short-duration planetary signals
- Sensitivity to free-floating and very wide-orbit planets
- Ability to compare planet occurrence across different Galactic environments and host-star populations

Together, these make space-based microlensing one of the best methods for completing the demographic census of cold planets, especially around low-mass and distant stars.
